e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a servant—someone who serves or stands under another’s authority. It is commonly rendered “servant” or “servants,” depending on how it functions in the sentence. The word is used broadly throughout the Old Testament, appearing 801 times, and can describe people serving human rulers as well as those presented as God’s servants. Its surrounding context determines whether the emphasis is on service, submission, or a person’s recognized role under authority.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “sacks,” referring to containers used as objects in the account of Joseph’s brothers. It appears 15 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all within Genesis 42–44. The word is used in connection with giving, opening, taking, and returning the sacks, and it also appears in commands concerning them. Its ordinary sense is therefore concrete and practical: sacks handled during the movement and exchange of grain.

Adlai is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as a proper name rather than a general vocabulary word with a stated definition. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:29. English renderings retain the name as “Adlai,” so the word identifies the person named in that passage rather than expressing an action, quality, or command. Its particular significance there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: bow self, (make) crooked., falsifying, overthrow, deal perversely, pervert, subvert, turn upside down.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “pervert”: to distort what is right, fair, or properly ordered. It describes an action that bends a matter away from its proper course, whether referring to judgment, circumstances, or the way things are arranged. The word occurs 11 times in the Old Testament, appearing in Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations, and Amos. Its use in different settings keeps the central idea consistent: something is wrongly altered rather than left in its proper condition.

gl: Ataroth , the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine
d: Ataroth , the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine

e.t: “Ataroth” is a place-name, referring to a location in the Old Testament. It appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers and Joshua, and each occurrence identifies the place by this name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs in accounts concerning the territories of Israel’s tribes and the boundaries of their allotted land. Because the available passages do not provide a definition or description of the place itself, its precise location and significance must be understood from the surrounding biblical passages.

gl: to lean idly , i.e. to be indolent or slack
d: to lean idly , i.e. to be indolent or slack

e.t: “Slothful” describes someone marked by a lack of diligence or active effort. It functions as an adjective, expressing a quality rather than naming a person or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Judges 18:9. Its basic sense points to inactivity and reluctance to act. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself describes a failure to show needed energy or readiness.

gl: incense (as increasing to a volume of smoke); hence a worshipper
d: incense (as increasing to a volume of smoke); hence a worshipper

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “suppliants”—people who bring a request or appeal. It functions as a noun describing those who seek help or present a plea. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing once in Ezekiel 8:11 and once in Zephaniah 3:10. Its use in these passages identifies people according to their act of appealing, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation being described.

This Hebrew word means “destruction,” referring to the loss or collapse of something. It identifies a destructive outcome rather than an action, person, or object. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing twice in Job and once in Proverbs. Its use is therefore limited but consistent: it describes a condition of devastation or ruin. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Pasach is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Pasach” rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:33. The name itself does not provide a broader quality, action, or idea to explain; it identifies a person. Its specific significance therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage, rather than on an independently stated definition.

This word means “gathered.” It describes the action of collecting things together, bringing them into one place or group. In its Old Testament uses, it functions as a verb and can describe the collection of abundant goods, the gathering of material, or the bringing together of things that were previously scattered. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being gathered and the surrounding sentence.

e.t: “Zin” is a proper place name, identifying a wilderness or region mentioned in Israel’s journey and later boundary descriptions. It functions as a geographical name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs ten times, chiefly in Numbers, with additional occurrences in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cruse,” referring to a container used to hold something. It appears seven times in the Old Testament, each time as the object involved in an action or statement. The word occurs in accounts involving David and Saul and in the story of Elijah and the widow, where the cruse is connected with provision. Its basic sense remains the same across these occurrences: a physical container whose contents are present, used, or preserved.

gl: to erect , i.e. create ; by extension, to procure , especially by purchase (causatively, sell ); by implication to own
attain, buy(-er), teach to keep cattle, get, provoke to jealousy, possess(-or), purchase, recover, redeem, × surely, × verily.
d: to erect , i.e. create ; by extension, to procure , especially by purchase (causatively, sell ); by implication to own

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “buy,” describing the act of obtaining something through a purchase. It is used for transactions involving people, land, and other possessions, so its ordinary sense concerns acquiring something as one’s own by payment or exchange. The word occurs 86 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about purchasing land and acquiring servants. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

gl: to shrink , i.e. thicken (as unracked wine, curdled milk, clouded sky, frozen water)
d: to shrink , i.e. thicken (as unracked wine, curdled milk, clouded sky, frozen water)

e.t: This Hebrew word means “settled.” It describes something that has become still, fixed, or no longer moving. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including descriptions connected with water, bodily formation, and conditions of darkness. Its use therefore points to a state in which something has settled into a definite condition rather than remaining in motion or change. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a single-occurrence term whose precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It appears in the Hebrew text at Genesis 8:22, and its identity is preserved as a distinct Hebrew word. Because no gloss, short definition, approved fallback meaning, or verse text is available here, it would be unsafe to assign an English sense. Its meaning must therefore be determined from fuller lexical and contextual information.

This Hebrew word refers to greatness—the quality of being exalted, powerful, or impressive. It describes a high level of prominence or honor rather than an ordinary measure of size. In its five occurrences in the Hebrew Bible, it appears in Daniel and concerns the elevated status or splendor associated with rulers and kingdoms. The word can therefore point to greatness as something publicly recognized and possessed by a person or realm, while its exact emphasis depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew verb expresses being “lifted,” describing an upward elevation of a person. In its four Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel, it is used as a predicate concerning someone who is lifted up in position or stature. The word therefore points to elevation rather than a physical object being moved. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains being “lifted.”

This Hebrew noun means “pot.” It names a physical vessel rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Psalms. Its basic lexical sense remains the same wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse determines how that pot functions in the sentence. No broader meaning is needed to understand the word itself.

gl: to spread (a bed); by implication, to refresh
d: to spread (a bed); by implication, to refresh

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses the action of “comfort.” It functions as an action word, describing comfort given or experienced rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Job and the Song of Solomon. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its consistent supported meaning is “comfort.”

gl: rupture , i.e. a pang ; figuratively, ruin
d: rupture , i.e. a pang ; figuratively, ruin

e.t: This Hebrew word means “breaking.” It refers to the experience or result of something being broken, and it functions as a concise expression for that condition or act. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament, once in Jeremiah and once in Ezekiel. In both occurrences, the English rendering is “breaking,” supporting this central sense. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Abez is the name rendered “Abez”; it functions as a proper name rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identification: it points to a particular named place or entity. This Hebrew word appears once in the Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 19:20. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s normal naming function can be stated, but the specific role it plays in that verse cannot be expanded beyond the name itself.

Arpad is the name of a place, rendered “Arpad” in the English Bible. It functions as a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew name occurs six times, all in the Old Testament: in 2 Kings, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The references place Arpad among named cities or kingdoms mentioned in connection with national power, conflict, or judgment, though the precise significance in each passage depends on its surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Shuah.” It identifies an individual listed in the genealogical records of Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Genesis 25:2 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:32. In both passages, it functions as the object of a birth or begetting statement, marking Shuah as a person within a family line rather than describing an action or quality.

e.t: This Hebrew verb is associated with “drink” and describes an action involving drink. In some sentences, “with” appears as part of the surrounding wording, so the precise English expression depends on the sentence. It occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Haggai. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the word’s exact force in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Shelomith.” It identifies people in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears seven times in seven verses, including references in Leviticus, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Ezra. Because the same name is used in genealogical and family records, its role is to identify a particular person in each passage; the individual must be distinguished by the surrounding genealogy and context.

This Hebrew word means “shame,” referring to disgrace or dishonor. It is a rare term in the Old Testament, occurring only once, in Exodus 32:25. That single occurrence supports understanding it as a word naming shame itself rather than an action or command. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the condition of being exposed to disgrace or dishonor.

This Hebrew word refers to “Saphir,” functioning as a name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Micah 1:11. Because the available wording identifies the term by name but does not provide a fuller lexical definition, its basic sense is the designation “Saphir.” The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what is said about it there; the word itself identifies the named entity.

This Hebrew word refers to “thoughts.” It is used for what exists within a person and can be examined or known by God. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in Psalms: Psalm 94:19 and Psalm 139:23. Its role is to identify inward thoughts as an object of divine knowledge and searching, rather than an outward action or spoken statement.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “error,” referring to something that is wrong or misleading. It names a condition or result rather than describing an action itself. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Nehemiah and once in Isaiah. Its use in speech-related relationships in Isaiah connects the idea with words or statements that lead people away from what is right. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains error.

This Hebrew word means “scatter,” describing the act of spreading people or things apart. It functions as an action word, pointing to separation and dispersal rather than gathering or keeping together. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of scattering. The word is connected there with other Hebrew terms in a relationship that presents it as the sentence’s action.

This Hebrew word refers to “ponds,” meaning bodies of still or collected water. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 19:10, so its normal meaning is known from this single occurrence rather than from a broad range of passages. As a noun referring to physical water places, it identifies ponds or water collections, while the precise force of the word in Isaiah depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: oh that! ; with leave , or if it please
d: oh that! ; with leave , or if it please

e.t: This Hebrew word is an interjection expressing an urgent or heartfelt appeal, rendered “Oh.” It draws attention to what follows and can mark a speaker’s strong emotion while asking, pleading, or responding. The word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in brief appeals and exclamations. Its exact force—whether urgent, sorrowful, or pleading—depends on the surrounding words and situation in each passage.
